newsitem.title: FRANCE: Crash probe focuses on Airbus instrument panel.
newsitem.headline: Crash probe focuses on Airbus instrument panel.

text.p: A magistrate investigating the 1992 crash of an Airbus airliner said in an interview published on Monday that the pilots may have confused two similar buttons on the instrument panel.
Magistrate Francois Guichard told the newspaper Le Figaro the key to the crash was that the plane was going down at 3,300 feet per minute, much faster than the pilots believed.

The Air Inter narrow-body Airbus A320 was approaching Strasbourg airport in eastern France on January 20, 1992 when it crashed into Sainte-Odile mountain, killing 87 of 96 people on board, including both pilots.
"The key element in the Mont Sainte-Odile case is the plane's abnormal descent rate. Nothing was recorded which allows to say if it was commanded willingly or unwillingly," he said.
"The crew wanted to go down four times slower but made a mistake that may have been induced by the instrument panel, which, by the way, was later modified by the aircraft maker.
"There was then one button commanding two different descent modes with a nearby twin button with a different aim," he said.

Guichard said that the pilots were inexperienced and had focused on the horizontal, rather than vertical, movement of the aircraft. Indications which should have alerted them to an abnormal descent rate were insufficient in a crisis.
No comment was immediately available from aircraft maker Airbus Industrie. Airbus has previously declined to comment on the judicial investigation.

Max Venet, one of two experts appointed by Guichard, has said he believes the plane's positioning system may have given wrong information that could have contributed to the disaster, according to Echo, an association of victims' relatives.
The other expert, Jean Belotti, is sticking to his finding that an equipment failure was not involved.

The Echo association has long sought to pin part of the blame on the Airbus consortium, which comprises French state-owned SNI Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG and Casa of Spain.

The initial 1993 accident investigation report ruled out equipment failure and pointed to human error. A subsequent 1994 report by Venet and Belotti modified these conclusions but came up with no firm findings on the cause of the crash.
